Let’s dive into Chapter 6: Tracking Progress—Building Awareness and Accountability.
So, once you’ve got the basics down—giving, saving, and spending—it’s time for the next step: tracking your progress. Now, don’t worry, this isn’t about strict accounting or complicated spreadsheets. It’s really about building awareness.
Think of tracking like keeping a garden journal. You’re not just jotting down what you’ve planted—you’re noticing patterns, celebrating growth, and learning from any setbacks along the way.
Tracking can be super simple. Maybe you mark your progress on a chart, color in a savings thermometer, or write quick notes in a family notebook. The main idea is to make progress visible and encourage everyone to reflect.
For example, after a month of using the three-jar system, you might sit down as a family and look at how much was given, saved, and spent. This isn’t about judgment—it’s about learning. What worked well? What felt tough? And what might you try differently next time?
To weave tracking naturally into your routine, here are a few gentle ideas:
First, use visual progress tools. Stickers, charts, or even drawings are great ways to show how close you’re getting to a goal.
Next, set aside regular review moments. Whether it’s once a week or once a month, take some time to talk about what’s in each jar—and, more importantly, why.
And don’t forget to celebrate milestones. When you reach a goal—like saving up for a family outing or making a special donation—pause and acknowledge the effort. Talk about what made it possible.
Here’s something to pay attention to: tracking helps kids—and adults—develop a real sense of accountability. When children see the results of their choices, they start to understand that little actions really do add up.
Imagine a child saving a bit each week and watching their savings jar slowly fill up. It’s a powerful lesson in patience and consistency. On the flip side, if spending gets out of hand, seeing an empty jar can spark a helpful conversation about priorities and planning.
And remember, it’s not about being perfect. Mistakes and missteps are a natural part of learning. If a child spends all their money on a toy and there’s nothing left for giving or saving, that’s not a failure—it’s a chance to talk about making different choices next time. The focus here is on growth, not guilt.
Tracking also opens the door to deeper conversations about values. Families can talk about not just how much was given, but why certain causes were chosen. Or they might reflect on what it felt like to save for something special, or whether a recent purchase brought lasting happiness.
These discussions help kids connect money management to their own sense of purpose and meaning.
So, here’s the key takeaway: tracking progress is a gentle, supportive way to build awareness and accountability. By making progress visible and reflecting on your choices, families and children can develop the skills and confidence they need to manage money thoughtfully—and with intention.
